title: Who is at the door?
hookLine: a lover knocks, says "it is I," and is sent away until he learns to answer "it is you" (Masnavi 1.3056ff)

cards: You knock on a door, and from inside someone calls: who is it? And you say, without thinking: it's me. As if me were the most obvious thing in the world.
Couples do it on the phone. Kids do it at the front door. Me!
We say it all day long: my plan, my turn, my way, my feelings about it. A new week starts today. It's called guests, and it's about who we let in.
And it begins at a door, with a very short story of Rumi's.

teach.b: It's in Book One of the Masnavi. A man comes to the door of the one he loves and knocks. From inside, the beloved asks: who are you?
He answers: it's I. And the beloved says: go away. This isn't the time.
There's no place at a table like this for someone raw. Remember raw from the chickpea? Not yet cooked, still hard, still full of himself.

For a whole year he travels, burning with the pain of separation, and in Rumi's words, the fire cooks him. Then he comes back. He paces around the house, afraid some careless word will slip out again.
He knocks. The voice inside asks: who is at the door? This time he says: it is you.
And the beloved says: since you are I, come in.
There isn't room in this house for two I's. The story works on a few levels. On the surface, it's about love between people: real love has less me in it.
But Rumi is talking about God. The seeker comes to the door full of himself, and the door stays shut. Only when the self has been cooked down, when he can say it is you, is there room.
Sufi teachers put it this way: it isn't that he disappears. It's that his I no longer stands between. That's a long road.
But there's a small version of it at any kitchen table: arriving with it's me, or arriving with it's you. Your line: it is you.

how: In Sufi teaching, this story is often told to describe the lessening of the ego on the way to God, and many readers also take it as a picture of selfless love between people.

o: someone who loves you no matter what you do
a close friend you have known since childhood
the one you love, who opens once you stop saying I

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: not yet cooked, still full of himself
the answer that opens the door

s: the lover is let in the first time he knocks
he says 'it's I' and is told there's no place for the raw.
the lover travels for a year before coming back
burning in separation, and cooked by it.
the beloved says there's no room in the house for two I's
since you are I, come in.

games.q: you've come back after a year away. you knock, and the voice inside asks: who is at the door? what do you say?
games.why: he says 'it is you', and the beloved lets him in: there isn't room in this house for two I's.

practice: Notice how often I or me shows up in your thoughts, even now: I'm doing this right, I'm tired, me, me. Each time, let it soften and pass like footsteps going by a door, and rest in what's here without the name tag.
If you pray, you can rest in God's presence without saying who you are.

wordCard.voice: Beloved. A lover says it's I and is turned away, then returns after a year and says it's you, and the beloved lets him in. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian: I, me. the word the lover has to stop saying at the door.

carryVoice: Your line: it is you. Less me, and more room. Day two hundred thirteen.
